78: The production floor is laid out in four zones that follow the order of the work: mixing and dough preparation, fermentation, baking and cooling, and storage. The example space is about 1,800 square feet in total, shared with the storefront, and the mixing zone is the first thing we protect inside it. It holds the spiral mixer at {{inv_amasadora}}, the dividing and shaping equipment and a sturdy work table, and it needs slip-resistant flooring, washable wall surfaces, a handwashing sink within reach and enough floor drains for daily washdowns. Mixers and ovens throw off a lot of heat, so ventilation matters here as much as for the ovens. We draw the flow so that raw ingredients move one way, from receiving through mixing to baking, and finished product never crosses back through the raw side; your health department will ask to see that on the plans.
79: Controlled fermentation is the logistical heart of the bakery. A proofer and retarder, which is a cabinet that holds dough at set temperature and humidity, costs {{inv_fermentacion}} in the plan, and it lets us stretch fermentation over a long, planned window instead of racing the clock. We shape and load the dough in the afternoon, hold it cold overnight and bake it fresh before the doors open, which moves the heaviest hours of work away from the moment the first guests walk in. Refrigeration completes the chain: space for the liquid sourdough starter, for pre-ferments made the day before and for butter, eggs and dairy. A well-planned retarder also smooths the schedule, because the same dough can come out in different batches through the morning.
80: Baking and cooling decide the quality of the finished loaf and are the biggest energy use in the building, so equipment choice deserves care. The plan carries a deck or rack oven at {{inv_horno}}. A deck oven, with its heavy stone or brick baking surface, is the classic choice for hearth breads with a crisp crust and an open crumb. A rack oven, where a full rack of trays rolls in, is more flexible for pastries and larger batches and cuts handling time during the busiest bake. Many bakeries end up with one of each, and the right mix depends on your menu. Whichever you buy, confirm with the equipment dealer and your utility whether it runs on gas or electricity and what the building needs to supply it. Baked goods then cool on stackable racks in a ventilated area away from direct drafts and from the customer line, before they are sliced, packed or loaded for delivery.
81: Flour and ingredient management needs a short list of reliable suppliers and a delivery schedule frequent enough to avoid running out, with every lot traceable. We set par levels for our main flours, such as high-protein wheat, whole-grain rye and a few specialty flours that change with the season and with what our wholesale customers ask for, and we review them weekly against actual production. Ingredients are stored in closed, labeled containers raised off the floor, in a dry, cool area, away from walls and from cleaning chemicals, so grain does not pick up moisture or pests. First in, first out applies to everything, and we date every opened bag. Because wheat, milk, eggs, tree nuts and sesame are all common in a bakery, allergen ingredients get their own labeled storage and their own scoops. Opening inventory is budgeted at {{inv_stock}}.
82: The weekly production calendar is built around three blocks of work. The production shift starts around 4 a.m., before the shop opens, and belongs to the most experienced baker: feeding the starter, mixing and shaping the long-fermentation breads, and loading the first bakes so bread is on the shelves when the doors open. The counter team arrives for opening and handles sales, the morning pastry bake and coffee, while the afternoon is for wholesale order preparation, prep for the next day's dough, cleaning and receiving deliveries. The workbook sizes this on its Staffing tab with the production shift as its own row, apart from the shop hours, and the plan runs {{plantilla_puestos}} people, or {{plantilla_jornadas}} full-time equivalents, over {{dias}} opening days a year, including the owner-baker who also handles quality control and administration. We build a schedule where a missed shift never means a missed bake.
83: Wholesale deliveries to cafes and restaurants need a plan of their own. Orders come in by text, email or an ordering app by an agreed cutoff the afternoon before, they are prepared and packed in the afternoon, and bread leaves early in the morning so it arrives before the customer's lunch service or breakfast rush, when a kitchen has time to receive it. For the first accounts the owner can deliver in a personal or cargo vehicle, which also builds the relationships; as the route grows, a dedicated vehicle with insulated, food-safe containers becomes worth considering, especially in warm months. We keep the route short and clustered, because a bakery loses money when a driver spends the morning in traffic, and we set clear terms with each account for minimums, delivery days, payment timing and returns. Wholesale sits inside the same bakery sales line as the counter in the workbook, so the delivery cost has to be covered by the overall margin.
86: The organization of an artisan bakery with its own production floor has to follow how the day really works: production begins in the early hours of the morning and the storefront opens a few hours later. Our model starts with {{plantilla_puestos}} people on the payroll, equal to {{plantilla_jornadas}} full-time equivalents, in clearly separate roles, so that production and customer service each get the attention they need. That size fits the example space, where the production floor, counter and storage share one commercial lease, and it lets us make sourdough, pastries and the small cafe line without building a structure the sales cannot carry.
87: The organization chart starts with the head baker, who in this plan is also the owner. This person is the central figure of the project, responsible for formulas, fermentation control, the sourdough starter and supervision of the whole production process. The head baker also leads food safety: the HACCP-based food safety plan, temperature and time logs, allergen controls, and the ongoing training of the production team. At least one person on the team should hold a Certified Food Protection Manager credential where the state or county asks for one. The head baker is hard to replace in an artisan bakery, because the distinctive quality of the product, and ultimately the value proposition against industrial competitors, depends on this technical knowledge, which is why we plan early on for a second baker who can cover that role.
88: The baker runs daily production under the head baker, weighing, mixing, dividing, shaping and baking. We look for at least a couple of years of experience in an artisan bakery, with comfort around sourdough, controlled fermentation and consistent results from batch to batch. The bakery assistant supports production with ingredient preparation, cleaning of tools and equipment, upkeep of the work area and basic baking tasks. This position is open to people with initial training or experience in food service, and it is the most accessible entry point to the team, and a natural place to grow future bakers from within.
89: The counter team, which includes baristas for the small cafe corner, handles guest service, direct sales, payments and restocking of the display case. On early mornings these team members can combine that work with receiving the first bakes and setting up the sales floor. Because the model includes wholesale to cafes and restaurants, at least one person at the counter needs the organizational skills to take wholesale orders, confirm delivery times and keep in regular contact with business customers. On weekends we add a weekend extra, and relief shifts cover vacations and days off, since the United States sets no federal vacation requirement and time off follows your own policy.
90: Pay is set to the local market and sits on top of a legal floor. The Staffing tab in the workbook shows the monthly pay of each role in the example: the head baker and owner, a baker, a bakery assistant, counter staff and baristas, a weekend extra and relief shifts. Replace those figures with going rates in your area. The federal minimum wage is $7.25 an hour, about {{salario_minimo_federal}} a year for a full-time position of {{horas_semana}} hours a week, and many states and cities set a higher minimum that applies instead; no line in the plan should fall below it. In year 1, labor cost is {{personal_a1}} including employer payroll taxes, or {{personal_pct}} of sales. We estimate payroll taxes at {{cargas_pct}} of wages, and your actual rate depends on your state and insurer. Employees are hired on a W-2 and paid through payroll, and tips are not modeled in the workbook.
91: The production schedule asks the baking team to start in the early hours of the morning, which is one of the main obstacles to hiring in this trade, so we plan for it openly. Full-time schedules are set at {{horas_semana}} hours a week over five days, which keeps most roles below the point where federal overtime pay begins for non-exempt employees, and we keep time and payroll records as the Fair Labor Standards Act requires. Federal law does not require a premium for early-morning hours, but some employers pay one to attract bakers, and you should check your state's rules. The production shift finishes by midday and a simple handoff to the counter team follows. The shop opens in the early morning and stays open through the evening or the close of the day, depending on what the neighborhood's traffic supports, and the plan's opening days are {{dias}} a year.
92: Our hiring approach puts demonstrable experience in artisan production first, along with tolerance for early starts and a commitment to quality. Retention comes from competitive pay for the local market, predictable schedules published in advance, a clear path to more responsibility and paid training in fermentation, sourdough management and pastry technique. Investing in training on food safety, allergens and quality control is what keeps the product consistent from one baker to the next and reduces the risk of depending on one technical person. We also cross-train the production team so that two people can run every station, which protects the schedule when someone is sick or leaves.
93: The structural challenge of this trade in the United States is finding and keeping skilled bakers who are willing to work through the night and early morning. Artisan bakeries compete for the same people with restaurants, hotel kitchens, grocery store bakeries and industrial plants, which often offer steadier hours. That calls for a clear offer to the worker: a professional workplace, real training, schedules posted in advance, a path from assistant to baker, and a culture that respects the craft. We do not cite a vacancy rate or a salary survey here, because published figures vary by region and source; we price our roles against local job postings. The viability of the project depends heavily on the owner's ability to build a stable team that keeps both operations and quality steady, day after day.
96: Total startup investment is {{inversion_total}}, of which {{capex}} goes into startup costs and {{fondo_maniobra}} into the working capital reserve, so the cash needed at opening is {{necesidad_caja}}. The professional equipment is the core of the spend: the deck or rack oven at {{inv_horno}}, the spiral mixer at {{inv_amasadora}} and the proofer and retarder at {{inv_fermentacion}}. The build-out of the space is {{inv_obra}}, and the electrical service upgrade the ovens may require is {{inv_electricidad}}, which depends on the building's existing service and is worth confirming with your utility before you sign a lease. These example figures are estimates for a commercial bakery in a second-generation space, and your own quotes will differ with your city, the state of the building and whether you buy equipment new or used.
97: The rest of the investment covers the display case and counter at {{inv_vitrina}}, point-of-sale and signage, launch marketing of {{inv_lanzamiento}} and opening inventory of {{inv_stock}}. On top of that comes working capital to bridge the gap between paying suppliers and collecting sales, plus a cash reserve for the first months. We fund the project with {{fondos_propios}} of our own money, or {{aportacion_pct}} of the cash needed, and a {{prestamo}} bank or SBA 7(a) loan at {{tipo_prestamo}} nominal interest over {{plazo_prestamo}} years, with an annual payment of {{cuota_anual}} (annual equivalent; the lender will set monthly payments). Lenders usually expect an owner equity injection, so we show it clearly. The plan is lender-ready, but approval is never guaranteed, and equipment financing is another route some bakeries use for ovens and mixers.
98: The revenue forecast for the first three years shows gradual growth as regulars build and wholesale accounts settle in. In year 1 we project revenue of {{ventas_a1}}, based on {{clientes_dia}} transactions a day at an average check of {{ticket}} over {{dias}} opening days, with the busiest days on weekends and holidays. Year 2 assumes volume growth of {{crecimiento_a2}}, for revenue of {{ventas_a2}}, once the neighborhood has adopted the bakery and the wholesale accounts are established. Year 3 adds a further {{crecimiento_a3}} for {{ventas_a3}}, bringing the production floor closer to its practical capacity. On an average opening day in year 1, that is {{ventas_dia}} in sales.
99: The workbook treats retail and wholesale as one bakery sales line, not as separate channels, and it does not model a split of the line between counter and wholesale. Wholesale carries lower margins per unit than the counter but adds volume and regularity, which helps us plan production and cut waste, and the scenarios in the workbook move transactions, average check and opening days. The average check is {{ticket}} before sales tax, or {{precio_menu}} with an example sales tax of {{sales_tax}} included. Sales tax treatment is different for each part of the line: in many states, bakery goods to take away are treated as exempt food while food eaten on the premises is taxed, and sales to a cafe that resells them go through a resale certificate. The "3-Year P&L" tab therefore has a column for the tax-exempt share of the line that you can edit, and you should confirm the rules with your state's tax agency.
100: The cost structure follows the pattern of a bakery. Raw materials are a larger share of cost for butter pastry, which uses butter, eggs and specialty ingredients, and a smaller share for sourdough bread, which is mostly flour, water and salt. In the plan, food cost is {{food_cost_comida}} of food sales and beverage cost is {{food_cost_bebida}} of beverage sales, packaging and disposables add {{consumibles_pct}} of sales, and card processing fees are {{tarjeta_pct}} of sales. Together, cost of goods is {{cogs_pct}} of sales and the gross margin is {{margen_bruto_pct}}, which has to absorb labor, rent, utilities and overhead. We treat these percentages as editable estimates, tracked against actual production and waste every week.
101: The second major cost is people. In year 1, labor is {{personal_a1}} including employer payroll taxes, or {{personal_pct}} of sales, spread across the head baker, a baker, a bakery assistant, counter staff and the relief hours. Occupancy is {{ocupacion_anual}} a year ({{alquiler_mes}} a month in base rent), or {{ocupacion_pct}} of sales; the example is base rent only, so if your lease passes through property taxes, building insurance or common-area charges, add them. Utilities are {{suministros_mes}} a month, a figure that reflects the ovens, insurance is {{seguros_anual}} a year and the marketing budget is {{marketing_anual}}. Together with depreciation of {{amortizacion_anual}} and loan interest of {{intereses_a1}}, total fixed costs in year 1 come to {{costes_fijos_a1}}.
102: Accounting break-even for this model is {{equilibrio_clientes_dia}} transactions a day, equal to {{equilibrio_ventas}} of revenue a year, compared with our year-1 plan of {{clientes_dia}} a day. That figure weighs fixed costs, including rent, payroll, utilities and depreciation, against the contribution of each sale. Cash break-even (loan payments in, depreciation out) is {{equilibrio_caja_clientes_dia}} transactions a day, or {{equilibrio_caja_ventas}} a year, so the margin of safety over cash break-even is {{holgura_caja_pct}}. The lowest cash balance in year 1 is {{saldo_minimo}}, reached in month {{mes_saldo_minimo}}, which you can trace on the "12-Month Cash Flow" tab. The first months are the weakest, because it takes time to build regulars and wholesale accounts.
103: Year-1 EBITDA is {{ebitda_a1}}, or {{ebitda_pct_a1}} of sales, and the pre-tax result is {{resultado_antes_impuestos_a1}}. After income tax at an effective {{impuesto_beneficios}}, net profit is {{resultado_neto_a1}} in year 1, {{resultado_neto_a2}} in year 2 and {{resultado_neto_a3}} in year 3. Project payback before debt is {{payback}}, and payback on startup costs alone is {{payback_capex}}. In the pessimistic scenario, with {{pesimista_clientes}} transactions a day at {{pesimista_ticket}} over {{pesimista_dias}} days, the pre-tax result is {{pesimista_resultado}}; in the optimistic one, with {{optimista_clientes}} transactions a day, it is {{optimista_resultado}}. The lowest debt service coverage ratio over the loan is {{dscr_min}}, against the {{dscr_objetivo}} lenders typically look for.
106: The first thing to settle is what kind of bakery you are opening. Cottage food laws let people sell certain low-risk foods made in a home kitchen, usually with limits on where and how they can sell and, in some states, on annual sales, and they are not what this plan covers. This plan is for a commercial bakery with its own production space, a storefront and wholesale to cafes and restaurants, which needs a license for a commercial food operation, issued by the local or state health department or, in some states, the state agriculture department. Because that depends on your state and the type of sales, ask both before you plan anything. On the business side, most owners choose a sole proprietorship or a limited liability company. The U.S. Small Business Administration notes that you are automatically a sole proprietor if you do business without registering as anything else, and that an LLC generally protects personal assets such as your home and savings from business liabilities. We also obtain an Employer Identification Number from the IRS, which is free and needed to hire employees, register a business license with the city or county and a seller's permit with the state, and file a DBA if we trade under a different name. An accountant or attorney can help choose the structure.
107: Before signing a lease, we confirm with the city that zoning allows a retail bakery or light food production at that address, and once the space passes its final inspections the city issues a certificate of occupancy. A build-out normally needs building permits for construction, electrical, plumbing and mechanical work. The health department reviews the plans for the layout, equipment, sinks and surfaces before construction, then inspects the space before it grants the food establishment permit, so we submit early. Health codes are based on the FDA Food Code, which each state adopts in its own way. Ovens need their own attention: ventilation for the baking area and the gas connection if the ovens run on gas, each with its permits under local code, plus a possible upgrade of the electrical service ({{inv_electricidad}}), which is coordinated with the utility. Timelines vary a great deal from one city to the next, so these steps go first on the schedule.
108: Sales tax is handled at the state and local level, and bakeries sit in a gray area. In many places, bakery goods and bread sold to take away are treated as exempt food, while items eaten on the premises, such as a croissant with coffee at the corner table, are taxed, and the line between the two varies by state. We register with the state tax agency to receive a seller's permit, collect the right tax at the register, and report each filing period. When a cafe or restaurant buys our bread to resell, the customer gives us a resale certificate and the sale is not taxed to them. The workbook uses an example sales tax of {{sales_tax}}, and its "3-Year P&L" tab has an editable tax-exempt share of the line; set it to what your state allows and confirm with the state tax agency or your accountant.
109: Wholesale brings federal food rules into play. A retail food establishment is exempt from FDA food facility registration, and the FDA defines one as an establishment whose primary function is selling food directly to consumers, meaning that its annual sales directly to consumers exceed its annual sales to all other buyers. A bakery whose sales to cafes and restaurants outgrow its counter sales would have to register, so we track the split and ask our attorney if it ever approaches that line. Packaged products and wholesale items need a proper label, with the ingredient list and the contents declared, and under federal law the nine major food allergens, which are milk, eggs, fish, crustacean shellfish, tree nuts, peanuts, wheat, soybeans and sesame, must be clearly identified. We also keep at least one Certified Food Protection Manager on the team, for example through ServSafe, and food handler cards for the rest of the staff where the state or county requires them.
110: Insurance and employment complete the legal checklist. We plan on general liability coverage, which landlords usually require, product liability for the food we sell wholesale, property coverage for equipment and stock, and workers' compensation, which is required in almost every state; the workbook budgets insurance at {{seguros_anual}} a year. As an employer, we follow federal and state rules from the first hire: Form I-9 to verify work eligibility, Form W-4 for withholding, state new-hire reporting and the safety practices OSHA expects, which matter around ovens, heavy lifting and early shifts. Check each requirement with your accountant, an attorney and your local authorities. A note for readers in the United Kingdom: register the food business with your local council at least 28 days before trading, which is free; most cold bread and bakery food to take away is zero-rated for VAT, while food eaten on the premises and hot takeaway food are charged at 20%; expect a hygiene inspection and a Food Hygiene Rating from 1 to 5 in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, and declare the 14 allergens.
113: Opening an artisan bakery with its own production floor is a real business opportunity built on a clear foundation. Interest in bread made with care, real ingredients and traditional methods keeps growing in many neighborhoods, and guests are willing to pay more for it. We do not lean on a national growth figure. We build our numbers from the ground up: {{clientes_dia}} transactions a day, an average check of {{ticket}} and {{dias}} opening days a year give year-1 revenue of {{ventas_a1}}, against a total startup investment of {{inversion_total}}. The proposition rests on what a neighborhood bakery can do that a supermarket cannot: be fresh, be local and be visibly made by people who care.
114: The business model combines two complementary ways to sell that reduce dependence on a single source of traffic. Direct sales at the counter earn higher margins and put us in direct contact with guests, while wholesale to cafes and restaurants brings steady production volume and lets us plan the day's baking around confirmed orders, which cuts waste. In the workbook both sit in one bakery sales line, so the scenarios move transactions, average check and opening days. That diversification matters most in the first months, when stable cash flow is critical for survival, and the pessimistic case of {{pesimista_clientes}} transactions a day shows how much room we have if the counter builds slowly.
115: The risks are significant but manageable with careful planning. Specialized equipment is the largest early expense and should be negotiated with suppliers who offer financing or with dealers who sell used equipment in good condition, ideally inspected by a technician. Production that starts in the early hours of the morning is a real operational demand and must be reflected in the labor budget and in how shifts rotate. Waste is the quiet cost of any bakery. We plan production against pre-orders and standing wholesale orders, discount the end-of-day items and donate unsold food to local food banks, where federal law offers protection to good-faith donors under the Bill Emerson Good Samaritan Food Donation Act, which cuts losses and builds goodwill in the neighborhood.
116: The roadmap to opening follows the phases of the opening checklist included with this kit. In Phase 1 - Business Setup we form the company, obtain an EIN, register for taxes, open a business bank account and choose insurance. In Phase 2 - Location & Permits we choose and validate the space, check zoning, review the lease and begin the health department plan review and building permits. In Phase 3 - Equipment we install the oven, mixer and proofer, and carry out the electrical and ventilation work, because the layout of the production floor decides how much the bakery can produce, and we fix that layout before any construction starts. In Phase 4 - Staff we hire and train the baking and counter teams. In Phase 5 - Marketing we set up Google Business Profile, Yelp and social media and contact the first wholesale prospects. In Phase 6 - First 90 Days we open, adjust the schedule to real demand and review the numbers weekly.
117: Our target customer is the household in a neighborhood with solid incomes and an interest in quality food, plus the independent restaurants and cafes nearby that want better bread than they can get from a distributor. That points to a marketing approach built on what makes the bakery different: local ingredients, natural sourdough, daily baking and personal service. We track a few simple numbers: transactions per day against our target of {{clientes_dia}}, the average check against {{ticket}}, the share of repeat guests and the number of active wholesale accounts. Distinctive packaging and a clear visual identity reinforce that positioning from the first day.
118: From a financial standpoint, the plan reaches accounting break-even at {{equilibrio_clientes_dia}} transactions a day, with a cash break-even of {{equilibrio_caja_clientes_dia}}, and a payback before debt of {{payback}}. The lowest debt service coverage ratio over the loan is {{dscr_min}}, compared with the {{dscr_objetivo}} lenders typically look for, and the lowest year-1 cash balance is {{saldo_minimo}}. The plan is lender-ready, but approval is never guaranteed, and your own results will depend on your costs and your location. Success will ultimately depend on the team's ability to keep bread quality consistent, control production costs and build lasting relationships with wholesale customers. Replace the example numbers in the workbook with your own, review the legal checklist with your local authorities and your accountant, and bring the plan to the bank with confidence.
